newsitem.title: USA: No easy answers to US options quote volume problem.
newsitem.headline: No easy answers to US options quote volume problem.

text.p: As the U.S. options industry gathered here to toast surging volume and strong growth, the four options exchanges met to find a solution to a nagging problem that could stifle the expansion, but no easy answers emerged, industry officials said Saturday.
The problem is that option quote vendors are increasingly struggling to keep up with the ever widening list of option contracts.
"The exchanges are concerned and are talking about it," said Paul Stevens, president of the Options Clearing Corp. "It is an issue."
Trading volume continues to surge. In April, volume rose 27.1 percent from April 1996, to 21,449,524 contracts, according to the Options Industry Council, an industry trade group.
But according to some industry studies, up to 40 percent of listed options issues have no open interest, or no contracts open.

Joseph Stefanelli, executive vice president of derivative securities at the American Stock Exchange (AMEX), said some of the solutions the AMEX is considering are to delist some rarely traded index options or to change the price change parameters specialists use for its auto quote system.

"We're looking at some of our sector index options to see whether or not there are some that we might consider delisting," he said in an interview. "Index options pump out more quotes than any other single product."
He said there at least three sector indices the AMEX is looking at as possible delisting candidates but declined to name them.
He added that all the exchanges are "very actively" looking at delisting individual option series when they have no open interest.
Exchanges may delist individual series, but they are hesitant to delist entire options classes for fear that another exchange will pick them up.

"There's a certain competitive dynamic to delisting options," said William Brodsky, head of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE). "We also recognize that we have tremendous appetite to bring on new products."
He said the exchanges are examining whether they can establish minimal standards on delisting.
Robert Greber, president of the Pacific Exchange (PCX), said the PCX has put a staff together to work on the quote problem, but added that all four exchanges have to work together.
"We have to do it as an industry," he said.
Joseph Rizzello, executive vice president at the Philadelphia Stock Exchange (PHLX), agreed, and said selective quoting might be one solution.
He said the PHLX had similar problems "for years" with its currency options but was able to cut traffic by 40 percent through selective quoting.
Whatever the exchanges do, time is of the essence.

New order-handling rules in the Nasdaq stock market are being phased in and creating more quotes on Nasdaq stocks, which has a ripple effect through the options. In July, the new rules will spread to 1,000 other Nasdaq stocks.
"The new order-handling rules at the Nasdaq are creating this tremendous flood of quotations on OTC stocks," Brodsky said.
He said about half the CBOE's options are on Nasdaq stocks.
The CBOE is working with the Securities and Exchange Commission on this situation because it is having some problems dealing with the changes, he said.
Greber noted that some of the PCX's busiest options are on Nasdaq stocks.
"This is a crisis," he said, referring to the quote problem.

Michael Schwartz, a managing director at Oppenheimer & Co and head of the Committee on Options (COOP), said the exchanges have agreed to reduce options quote traffic by 25 percent but the order-handling rules changes will boost volumes by 22 percent.

"There doesn't seem to be an immediate answer," he said, adding that the quote vendors, who include Reuters Holdings Plc, Bloomberg LP and Shark Information Services, may have to increase their capacity.
"The final question is, who's going to pay?," he asked.
